caption:
OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki wants AI labs to agree on a shared speed limit.
His yardstick is perplexity, a score for how well a model predicts the next token.
Labs would not push past a common threshold until they can better monitor what AI does.

Should AI companies agree to slow down together?

paragraphs.text: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published a post on November 22, 2026 titled Perplexity and Intelligence, in which he proposes that leading AI developers agree on common limits to how far they push their models. TechCrunch reported on the post that afternoon, and Datastudios published a detailed summary of its figures.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman praised the post on X, describing it as the most important thing the company had published in a while, according to TechCrunch.

Pachocki argues that benchmarks built around specific downstream tasks have gone out of date as models improved, while perplexity has stayed informative. Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average, and a lower score means better predictions. TechCrunch reported that the post includes a chart showing how the perplexity of OpenAI's models has fallen since GPT-3.5.

According to Datastudios, the figures are log-perplexity scores measured on a held-out dataset drawn from OpenAI's internal codebase. GPT-3.5 sat at roughly 0.99 and GPT-4 at roughly 0.91. Pachocki wrote that GPT-4 was able to use chain-of-thought reasoning productively at that level, and that once OpenAI's models reached losses below 0.8, the company saw transformative capabilities emerge in fields such as cybersecurity and mathematics.

Datastudios reported that the post also cites an unnamed OpenAI model at about 0.76, linked to strong results on open math problems, and expects further capability jumps somewhere around 0.68 to 0.7. The post does not say which model reached 0.76 or whether the lower range would serve as a limit.
What the proposal asks of AI labs

Pachocki suggests that perplexity could act as a shared benchmark for general intelligence, which companies could use to set common limits. Under the idea, developers would commit not to go past an agreed threshold until their ability to understand and monitor AI behavior reaches a concrete milestone, TechCrunch reported.

Datastudios described the plan in three layers: shared norms for evaluating and red-teaming frontier models before first use, along with transparency standards; commitments not to cross common limits defined by perplexity and other measures until a monitoring milestone is met, with a successor to chain-of-thought monitors given as an example; and a framework for setting later limits. The post names no partner companies and no date for a first limit, and it announces no change to ChatGPT, Codex or the API, according to Datastudios.

The post also lists open problems, Datastudios reported. Labs train on different datasets, perplexity does not map directly onto real tasks, gains from chain-of-thought reasoning do not lower perplexity, and nobody knows where the loss floor lies. OpenAI said it is publishing its own numbers as a first step, while acknowledging that this gives competitors a clearer view of its progress.

The proposal arrives as calls for restraint grow inside the industry. TechCrunch noted that Anthropic's IPO filing warned the technology could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society, and that Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has published a plan to pace the frontier, calling for common safety standards and limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress. Altman and Elon Musk reportedly endorsed that plan.

The notable part is less the idea of limits than the choice of a single number to define them. A shared metric would let rival labs check one another, but only if they agree on the dataset it is measured on, a problem the post itself raises. By publishing its own scores first, OpenAI is betting that openness will pull competitors into the same frame.
The test is whether Anthropic, Google DeepMind, xAI or Meta publish comparable perplexity figures or sign on to a common threshold. Without that, the proposal remains one company's yardstick.
